the rate of force development is not related to the level of MLC phosphorylation, and that basal and initial levels of MLC phosphorylations play a cooperative role.
the rate of force development is not dependent on myosin light-chain phosphorylation.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of ATP reduction on phosphorylation of myosin light chains in intact arterial smooth muscles and the relationship between myosin light-chain phosphorylation and force development.

the effects of ATP depletion on the pattern of myosin light-chain phosphorylation (MLC) during contraction and the relationship between force development and MLC phosphorylation in intact carotids from rabbits.
the role of the 20-kilodalton (20-kDa) light chain of smooth muscle myosin (myosin light chain) in force generation and maintenance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between MLC phosphorylation and force development is not simple.
the rate and magnitude and the extent of MLC phosphorylation are not related.
the relationship of force development to phosphorylation is not a linear function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate of force generation is related to the amount of MLC phosphorylation, but that the magnitude of force development is not.
MLC phosphorylation is a prerequisite for the generation of force but is not a rate-limiting step.

ATP reduction in intact arterial smooth muscles does not affect the maximal force development but does affect the pattern of force generation, and that this effect is related to a change in the phosphorylation of MLC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate of force development is independent of MLC phosphorylation and is determined by the rate of Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the Ca2+ binding affinity of myofilaments.
MLC phosphorylation and force development are independent processes.
the phosphorylation of the light chains of myosin is not the only factor that determines the force developed in smooth muscle.
